timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Three kinds of attackers? Isn't a hacker a hacker?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Insiders, external actors, and supply chains. Different origins, different controls.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Insiders first. They already have access, right?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Yes. Least privilege, UEBA to spot odd behavior, DLP on sensitive data, separation of duties.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Layered defenses, XDR feeding a SIEM, SOAR to automate response, and tested incident plans.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: What makes supply chain attacks different?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: You're trusting someone else's code. Verify with code signing and SBOMs, assess vendors before onboarding.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Do third parties get full access?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Least privilege only, and isolate their integrations with segmentation.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: What's the common thread across all three?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Assume breach, monitor continuously, and automate containment with tested response.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Assume breach again. It keeps coming up.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Because prevention eventually fails. Design so the damage stays small when it does.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So I need all three playbooks written down?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Documented and drilled. A plan nobody tested is just a document.
